t: Closest Dessert Cost via Topping Choice Enumeration
o: Pick exactly one base, then add each topping 0, 1, or 2 times, so a dessert cost is base plus a weighted topping sum; we minimize |cost - target| and break ties toward the smaller cost. Because n, m are at most 10, there are at most 3^10 = 59049 topping combinations per base - tiny. Example 1 hits 10 exactly (base 7 + one topping worth 3). Example 2 shows why overshoot control matters: 17 beats 20 because it lies closer to 18. Example 3 stresses the tie rule: costs 8 and 10 are equally close to 9, and the lower one, 8, is returned.
k: Each topping contributes independently 0, c, or 2c - a ternary choice per topping, so DFS over 3^m leaves is feasible for m <= 10.
Track the best candidate lexicographically by (|cost - target|, cost): strictly closer wins, equal distance prefers the cheaper dessert.
Bases and toppings decouple: enumerate achievable topping sums once, then combine with every base (the DP view).

a.i: Fix a base, then recursively decide each topping multiplicity in {0, 1, 2}. At a leaf compare the running total against the best using the statement comparison. Repeat for every base; recursion depth is only m <= 10.
s: For each base b, launch dfs(i = 0, sum = b).
At topping i branch into sum, sum + c_i, sum + 2*c_i.
At i = m update best by (distance, cost) preference.
a.t: O(n*3^m) - each of n bases roots a ternary recursion tree over m toppings

a.n: Approach 2: DP Over Achievable Topping Sums
a.i: Compute the set of all reachable topping totals bottom-up: start from {0} and extend every existing sum by k*c for k in {0,1,2}. The set automatically merges duplicates - different topping mixes with equal price collapse to one state - shrinking the search space versus blind enumeration. Then try every (base, sum) pair and keep the best under the same comparison rule.
s: For each topping c, replace reachable with all sums s + k*c, k in {0,1,2}.
For each base b and each sum s, evaluate candidate b + s.
Keep the candidate minimizing (|cand - target|, cand).
a.t: O(n*S) where S is the number of distinct topping sums, bounded by 3^m but usually far smaller after deduplication

w: Interview pick: the DFS (approach 1) - shortest to explain - offering the DP as a dedup refinement. Watch the tie-break direction (lower cost wins on equal distance, example 3), remember toppings are entirely optional, and that exactly one base is mandatory. Pruning the DFS once cur exceeds target + current best distance speeds things up but is unnecessary at these sizes. Follow-up: many toppings would call for meet-in-the-middle or a bitset over achievable sums.
